name: Vegetarian and pescatarian diets
lead: Vegetarian diets exclude meat, and pescatarian diets exclude meat but include fish and seafood; both may include eggs and dairy [11][17]. The term "pescetarian" was coined in the United Kingdom in the late 1980s, and surveys in 2017-2018 estimated that about 3 percent of adults worldwide followed the diet [11]. People in appearance-focused communities discuss these diets as ways to eat leaner, to lower the saturated-fat load of a diet, and, in the case of pescatarians, to keep the omega-3 fats and protein of fish while skipping red meat.

The appearance case for these diets runs through body composition and general health: observational studies find that vegetarians and vegans on average have lower body mass index, cholesterol and blood glucose than omnivores, and a leaner physique is the visible result that dieters seek [12]. At the same time, communities such as looksmax.org debate whether meat-free eating affects growth, jaw development, muscle and skin, and they often treat fish as a middle path [19][20].

Research on vegetarian and pescatarian diets is large but mostly observational, covering cancer, cardiovascular risk factors, micronutrient status and diet quality. A UK Biobank cohort of 409,110 people and a meta-analysis examined meat, vegetarian, pescatarian and fish-poultry diets and cancer risk; a Swiss population study linked these diets to cardiovascular risk factors; and several studies of 16 to 24 year olds compared micronutrient status across diets [1][2][4][8][10]. Dietetic bodies such as the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics state that properly planned vegetarian diets are nutritionally adequate [17][18].

paras: Lacto-ovo vegetarians eat dairy and eggs; lacto vegetarians eat dairy but not eggs; ovo vegetarians eat eggs but not dairy; vegans eat no animal products; flexitarians eat mostly plants with occasional meat or fish [11]. Pescatarian diets are close to Mediterranean-style eating, which features fish and plants [11]. Wikipedia also lists pollotarianism (poultry but not red meat) among semi-vegetarian patterns and notes that the Vegetarian Society rejects semi-vegetarian labels for its own definition [17].

Definitions vary between organizations. A 2023 review of how health bodies define "plant-based" and "vegetarian" diets proposed standard definitions because the terms are used inconsistently [15]. A 2024 study of young people in Norway and a 2025 study in Sweden each compared vegans, lacto-ovo vegetarians, pescatarians, flexitarians and omnivores as separate groups [4][10]. The motives for following these diets include ethics, religion, health, environment, economics and taste [17], and reviews such as a 2023 European Heart Journal paper weigh the benefits and drawbacks of vegetarian and vegan eating [16].

Wikipedia traces the earliest record of vegetarianism to Jain tradition, with Parshwanatha and later Mahavira reviving ahimsa (non-harm) between the 9th and 6th centuries BCE, and to Greek vegetarian theory from the 6th century BCE, including the Orphics and Pythagoreans [17][11]. In 675 CE Emperor Tenmu of Japan restricted the killing and eating of livestock, and in 737 Emperor Shomu approved eating fish and shellfish; medieval European monastic orders such as the Benedictines restricted meat but generally ate fish [11][17].

The word "vegetarian" first appeared around 1838-1841, associated with Alcott House in London; the Vegetarian Society was founded in Manchester in 1847 and the International Vegetarian Union in 1908 [17]. Francis William Newman, president of the Vegetarian Society from 1873 to 1883, made associate membership possible for non-strict vegetarians and in the 1890s switched to a diet that included fish [11]. The word "pescetarian", a blend of the Italian pesce and "vegetarian", was coined in the UK in the late 1980s, and the synonym "pesco-vegetarian" has appeared in American publications since at least 1980 [11]. A 2016 book, Seagan Eating, promoted a seafood diet that excludes dairy and eggs [11].

A 2018 Ipsos MORI report put pescetarians at 3 percent of adults worldwide, a figure matched by a 2017 GlobalData survey; the same 2018 survey found 5 percent in Africa and the Middle East, and a 2020 seven-nation European survey put the EU average near 3 percent [11]. UK polls found 4 percent in 2018 and 3 percent in 2021, and pescetarianism is more common among women than men in every region with data [11]. India has the highest share of vegetarian residents of any country, followed by Mexico, and several Indian towns have banned meat sales [17].

The Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2020-2025 list a healthy vegetarian pattern as one of three recommended healthy eating patterns, and the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics states that a properly planned vegetarian diet is healthful and nutritionally adequate and may help prevent and treat certain diseases [17]. A 2021 systematic review of 141 studies found that protein intake was lower in plant-based dieters than in meat-eaters but well within recommended levels, that fiber, folate, vitamin C, vitamin E and magnesium intake was higher, and that EPA and DHA intake was lower [14]. The same review reported that intake and status of vitamin B12, vitamin D, iron, zinc, iodine and calcium were generally lower in plant-based groups [14].

Wikipedia reports that the idea that vegetarians must combine grains and beans at the same meal has never been substantiated, and that Frances Moore Lappe withdrew the claim in later editions of Diet for a Small Planet starting in 1981; good plant protein sources include soy products, other legumes, nuts, seeds and cereal grains [18]. Eggs and dairy add protein for lacto-ovo vegetarians, and fish adds it for pescatarians [11][17].

Vegetarians tend to have lower iron stores and a higher risk of iron deficiency anemia, because plant iron is non-heme and absorbed less efficiently; the Academy recommends roughly 1.8 times the iron intake of non-vegetarians, and vitamin C improves absorption while phytates, tea polyphenols and calcium reduce it [17][18]. A 2013 review cited by Wikipedia found lower zinc intake and serum concentrations in vegetarian populations [18]. Vitamin B12 is found mainly in animal foods; eggs and dairy provide some, while vegans need fortified foods or supplements, and the Academy recommends B12 supplements for everyone over 50 [17][18].

Plant foods such as flaxseed, chia and walnuts provide ALA but little EPA or DHA, whereas fish supply EPA and DHA directly [18][11]. A 2022 review cited on Wikipedia found that microalgal oil reliably raised DHA and EPA, while flaxseed or echium oil did not [18]. Studies of Scandinavian young people included carotenoid and fatty-acid biomarkers in their comparison of plant-based and omnivorous diets [8].

A 2025 meta-analysis of 59 studies covering 48,626 young people, cited on Wikipedia, found that well-planned vegetarian diets support healthy growth but carry a risk of shortfalls in B12, vitamin D, calcium, iron and zinc [17]. A 2009 TARGet Kids study reported that vegetarian and vegan children were twice as likely to be underweight as meat-eating children [18]. Wikipedia notes that the link between ethnicity and underweight status in that study is unknown [18].

Pescatarian eating keeps fish and shellfish, which supply protein and the long-chain omega-3 fats EPA and DHA [11][18]. Wikipedia describes pescatarian diets as overlapping with the Mediterranean diet, which is linked to lower cardiovascular disease risk, and says pescatarian diets are under preliminary study for effects on diabetes, long-term weight gain and mortality [11]. Wikipedia also notes concerns about mercury and PCBs in some fish, and that choosing low-mercury species or limiting high-mercury fish lowers exposure [11].

Environmental analyses cited by Wikipedia estimate that pescatarian diets cut greenhouse gas emissions by about 45 percent compared with omnivorous diets in a 2014 life-cycle analysis, and by 64 percent in overall environmental impact in a 2020 study [11]. A 2023 American study of self-selected popular diets found wide variation in carbon footprints and diet quality across vegetarian, pescatarian and other diets [3].

A 2017 meta-analysis of 86 cross-sectional and 10 prospective cohort studies found lower body mass index, total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol and glucose in vegetarians and vegans than in omnivores, and, in cohort studies, a lower risk of ischemic heart disease (relative risk 0.75) and of total cancer incidence (0.92), without a significant difference in all-cause mortality [12]. A 2023 meta-analysis of 30 randomized trials found that vegetarian or vegan diets lowered total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein B compared with omnivorous diets [13]. A 12-week randomized trial in African American adults compared the Healthy US, Mediterranean and vegetarian patterns of the US Dietary Guidelines for body weight, hemoglobin A1c, blood pressure and diet quality [23].

In the UK Biobank analysis of 409,110 participants, researchers compared diet types with all-cancer and site-specific cancer incidence and combined the results with a meta-analysis of prospective cohorts [1]. The Swiss study examined prevalence, sociodemographic features and cardiovascular risk factors among vegetarian, pescatarian and flexitarian dieters [2]. Studies of Norwegian and Swedish 16 to 24 year olds compared micronutrient intake and status, and food groups and biomarkers, across vegan, lacto-ovo vegetarian, pescatarian and omnivorous diets [4][8][10]. Other studies cover nutritional status and habits, thrombotic risk factors and erectile function with organic and fasting regimens [5][6][7], and modelling research examined diets with reduced animal protein [9].

In general terms, people following these diets build meals around legumes, soy products, grains, nuts, dairy and eggs (for lacto-ovo vegetarians), and fish or seafood (for pescatarians). The Academy and other bodies note that vegans and many vegetarians rely on fortified foods or supplements for vitamin B12, and Wikipedia lists algae-based EPA/DHA supplements as an option for those who avoid fish [17][18]. Nutrition researchers studying young adults measured intake and blood or urine biomarkers to see whether dieters meet requirements [4][10].

These diets appear on looksmax.org mostly as questions about whether meat-free eating helps or hinders appearance. One thread asks whether a vegetarian diet is unhealthy, drawing replies that veganism is "fine" and one poster who would go pescatarian "if I had to" because of fish [19]. A thread by a poster raised on a lacto-vegetarian Indian diet argues that meat-eating Indians tend to be taller with better facial structure, and replies credit chewing meat with jaw development [20]. Another thread asks how badly a vegetarian diet stunted growth [22]. A vegan poster in a different thread reports low body fat, athletic performance and no acne [21].

The studies identified are mostly observational or cross-sectional, covering cancer, cardiovascular risk factors, micronutrient status and diet quality [1][2][4][5][8][10], alongside randomized trials and meta-analyses of blood lipids and weight outcomes [13][23]. No clinical trial has tested vegetarian or pescatarian diets for skin or facial appearance.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, vegetarian and pescatarian diets come up as questions about growth, jaw development and skin, with fish often presented as a compromise [19][20][22].

claims.claim: A vegetarian childhood stunts height and facial growth.
claims.believers: A poster raised on a lacto-vegetarian Indian diet says he believes he would be 2-3 inches taller and have more forward facial growth without it; another thread asks how badly vegetarian eating stunted growth [20][22].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports a 2025 meta-analysis of 59 studies finding that well-planned vegetarian diets support healthy growth but risk shortfalls in B12, vitamin D, calcium, iron and zinc; a 2021 review found those nutrients generally lower in plant-based groups [17][14].

claims.claim: Chewing meat builds the jaw and drives forward maxillary growth.
claims.believers: A reply in the Indian-diet thread says a "meat bolus" widens the jaw and pushes the maxilla forward [20].
claims.experts: No study cited in this article tested meat chewing against jaw or maxillary development; the nutrition studies measured intake and biomarkers [4][14].

claims.claim: Pescatarian eating is the best compromise because fish carries "too much benefit" to skip.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster says they would choose pescatarian if they had to because of fish [19].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes fish is part of the Mediterranean diet, which is linked to lower cardiovascular disease risk, and also notes mercury and PCB concerns in some fish [11].

claims.claim: Vegetarianism and veganism lead to "nutritional suicide".
claims.believers: A thread opener asks whether vegetarianism shares the problems he attributes to veganism, and replies debate whether the stigma is deserved [19].
claims.experts: The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics states that properly planned vegetarian diets are nutritionally adequate, while a 2021 review reports generally lower B12, vitamin D, iron, zinc, iodine and calcium status in plant-based groups [17][14].

claims.claim: A plant-based diet gives low body fat, athletic performance and clear skin.
claims.believers: A vegan poster reports low body fat, fast running times and no acne, and says this predates the diet [21].
claims.experts: A 2017 meta-analysis found lower BMI in vegetarians and vegans than omnivores; no clinical trial has tested these diets for skin appearance [12].

card.summary: Reduced-meat diets with decent population data on health but nothing on looks.
card.note: Some fish contain mercury; vegetarians should watch B12 and iron.

quick.overview:
Vegetarian diets exclude meat; pescatarian diets add fish and seafood. Both are common, moderate alternatives to omnivorous or vegan eating.

Studies are observational and focus on cancer, cardiovascular risk and nutrient status; none test appearance.
quick.mechanism: They shift intake toward plants and, for pescatarians, fish-derived omega-3. Any effect on skin or leanness is untested.
quick.risks: Nutrient status studies compare B12, iron and others across diets; some fish carry mercury and PCBs.

chain: Swap meat for plants, eggs, dairy or fish
Different intake of calories, fats, fiber, protein and micronutrients
Observational links to lower BMI and cholesterol
A leaner physique, with nutrient planning to cover B12, iron, zinc and omega-3
angle.text: People adopt vegetarian or pescatarian eating to lean out, to shift fat intake and to follow ethical or religious practice. Observational studies associate vegetarian diets with lower body mass index; how this affects facial or skin appearance specifically has not been tested.
